title: What Is Kundalini? Meaning, Origins, and Myths
h1: What Is Kundalini? Meaning, Origins, and Myths
excerpt: Kundalini is a traditional image of latent spiritual power, not a laboratory finding and not identical to every modern class.

quick_answer.question: What is kundalini?
quick_answer.answer: Kundalini is a concept in some Indian yogic and tantric traditions naming a latent power, often pictured as coiled energy. Traditions disagree about it, and science has not established the picture as anatomy.

intro: Kundalini is a traditional metaphor that American marketing often treats as a body part. The metaphor can be explained. The body part has not been demonstrated.

sections.heading: What does kundalini mean?
sections.content:
The word is tied to shakti, the language of power, and to images of coiling and rising. Inside those traditions the aim is a change in awareness, not a spectacle. There is no single ancient checklist called an awakening that every text shares. Britannica's article is a calmer public summary than a symptom thread.

The neighboring page is [the kundalini topic](/topics/kundalini/). Treat that link as part of the argument, not as decoration.

sections.heading: Where does the image come from?
sections.content:
Tantric and hatha literature developed subtle-body maps with channels and centers. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika is one public window, not a beginner's script. Later English interpreters systematized the images. Systematizing is authorship and should be labeled as such.

A wider map lives at the [chakras topic](/topics/chakras/). Dates and school names matter, because a recent American presentation is often described as if it had no date.

sections.heading: What do modern classes add?
sections.content:
People report heat, movement, emotion, and sleep changes. Reports are reports. Similar sensations have ordinary medical causes. A studio class called Kundalini Yoga is largely a twentieth-century teaching, described on its own page, not the whole archive. Do not chase an experience because a video promised bliss.

If you want a narrower practical or comparative page, use [kundalini for beginners](/articles/kundalini-for-beginners/). You can understand the description without joining a group or buying a course.

sections.heading: What should a careful reader refuse?
sections.content:
No scientific consensus establishes a serpent energy. Intense breathing can make you dizzy without proving a mechanism. If you cannot sleep or function, see a clinician. A teacher who calls all distress a spiritual test is asking you to skip ordinary safety.

Readers in the United States often meet a simpler version of the same idea in a class, an app, or a short video. Name that simpler version instead of pretending it is the whole tradition. Traditional teaching, personal report, and research stay in separate sentences on this site. The [editorial policy](/editorial-policy/) is the rule. The [disclaimer](/disclaimer/) applies whenever a sentence leans toward health, safety, or a promised transformation. The [corrections](/corrections/) page is how to challenge a factual mistake. Name the school, the text, or the century whenever a sentence would otherwise float free of history. A reader may stop at the definition when that is all the question required.

key_takeaways: Kundalini is a traditional concept, not an anatomical organ.
Texts and modern classes do not match one script.
Reports of sensation are not proof of a mechanism.
Safety belongs with ordinary medical sense.
